ai_summary:
Current power network dynamics highlight Scotland's exceptional renewable capacity alongside the ongoing operational challenges posed by cross-border transmission bottlenecks. Great Britain wind output currently stands at 12.9 GW, with estimated Scottish wind output delivering 4.6 GW, representing 45.5% of installed Scottish wind capacity. Driven by this strong renewable generation, Scottish carbon intensity has dropped to 0 gCO2/kWh, demonstrating a stark regional divergence from the GB-wide figure of 134 gCO2/kWh.

However, network transfer limits prevent this surplus zero-carbon power from reaching southern demand centers. Consequently, Scottish generation curtailed so far today has climbed to 24659.9 MWh, resulting in a substantial constraint cost of about £594,209. To replace this stranded volume and maintain whole-system balance, thermal plants elsewhere must be dispatched. The estimated gas burned elsewhere to replace it has reached 4685381.0 m3, which adds an unnecessary 8631.0 tonnes CO2 to the atmosphere. This operational friction illustrates a costly inefficiency in the national grid, where consumers shoulder substantial balancing payments while the forced suppression of Scottish wind directly drives up thermal fuel consumption and counteracts national decarbonization efforts.
